Gaius
GAY-us
proper noun
From the common Roman name Gaius, borne by a host of the apostle Paul and a beloved friend of the apostle John.

See also: Gaius

Biblical Definition

Gaius is a name borne by more than one believer in the New Testament, chiefly remembered as a host and helper of the apostles. At Corinth there was a Gaius whom Paul himself baptized, and who became the apostle’s host and a host of the whole church, opening his house to the gathered saints; Paul sends his greeting in the Epistle to the Romans, Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you (Rom 16:23), and names him among the few he baptized with his own hand (1Co 1:14). And the apostle John wrote his third epistle to a beloved Gaius, commending him for his faithful hospitality to the travelling preachers of the gospel: Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers (3Jo 1:5), adding that we ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth (3Jo 1:8). The dictionary marks Gaius as the pattern of Christian hospitality, the open house and open heart that receive the servants of Christ and so share in their labour. Whether the Corinthian host of Paul or the beloved of John, the men who bore this name are honoured for ministering to the saints; and they teach that to lodge and help the messengers of the gospel is itself a fellowship in the truth they carry, and a service the Lord remembers.

Webster 1828 Definition

A New Testament name borne by hosts of the apostles, a pattern of Christian hospitality to the servants of Christ.

expand to see more

GAIUS, a common Roman name borne by several New Testament believers.

A Gaius of Corinth was baptized by Paul and hosted the whole church.

Paul greets him in Romans as “mine host, and of the whole church.”

The apostle John wrote his third epistle to a beloved Gaius.

He is commended for his hospitality to travelling preachers.

Key Scripture

Rom 16:23 — "Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother."

1Co 1:14 — "I thank God that I baptized none of you, but Crispus and Gaius;"

3Jo 1:5 — "Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers;"

3Jo 1:8 — "We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth."

Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture; the pattern of Christian hospitality, whose open house received the servants of Christ.

expand to see more

Gaius has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the host of Paul at Corinth and the beloved friend of John. The dictionary records the name that the reader may mark the hospitality for which these believers are honoured in the New Testament.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the grace of Christian hospitality, the open house and open heart that receive the servants of Christ. Gaius of Corinth was host to the whole church; the beloved Gaius of John’s epistle dealt faithfully with the brethren and with strangers, lodging the travelling preachers of the gospel. The apostle teaches that we ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth; for to lodge and help the messengers of the gospel is itself a fellowship in the truth they carry. The men named Gaius teach the church that hospitality to the saints is no small service, but a sharing in their labour that the Lord remembers.

From the common Roman name Gaius, the name marks the hospitable hosts of the apostles Paul and John.
